extracted.intended_audience: law students, maritime/international law practitioners, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes legal standards about the effect of war on commercial relations, property, contracts, and persons (domicile, ships, cargoes, insurance, bills, partnerships, prisoners) from a legal-treatise style text. Useful for applying or teaching international and maritime law principles in wartime contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading with the enemy — confiscation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Trading with the enemy, except under a Royal Licence, subjects the property to confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Government authorises a homeward trade but not an outward trade intimately connected with it, the latter may be confiscated. Cargoes laden before the war may be condemned if parties did not use all diligence to countermand the voyage after notice of hostilities. British merchants should apply to their Government for special importation when withdrawing property from enemy country; this is the safe way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects of an ally may not trade with the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: During a Conjoint War no Subject of an Ally can trade with the common enemy without liability to forfeiture of all property engaged in such trade in the prize courts of the Ally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relaxation of this rule can occur only by permission of the sovereign power or by mutual consent of the allied nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts with the enemy during war are void
rubrics_metrics.description: All Contracts made with the Enemy during War are utterly void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to insurances on the enemy's property and trade, drawing and negotiation of bills of exchange (whether the acceptor is a subject or alien enemy), sending money or bills to the enemy's country, commercial partnerships, and all endeavours to trade by third persons. Contracts made in contemplation of war to evade belligerent rights are also illegal, even if made by neutrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurances void when protecting enemy interests or illegal voyages
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal or common law of every state declares insurances void by which ships or merchandise of the enemy are sought to be protected; insurances by or on behalf of alien enemies are wholly illegal and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both the policy and the loss occurred before war, the remedy is only suspended during the war. The general principle is that the contract of assurance is vacated ab initio wherever an insurance is made on a voyage expressly prohibited by common, statute, or maritime law. If a licence is not strictly pursued and the voyage becomes illegal, the insurance is void. The validity of a policy is tested by the voyage (if voyage prohibited by law on public policy grounds), not by the will of the parties; an underwriter told of illicit voyage is not more bound than if not told. Policies to broad descriptions (e.g., 'ports in the Baltic') may be legal because some ports may not be hostile. Neutral vessels carrying contraband have issues based on cargo rather than voyage. Insurances are good on neutral vessels engaged in the colonial trade of the enemy that was closed to neutrals in peace, subject to tracing of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of exchange with the enemy — voidness and limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: All Bills drawn or negotiated with the enemy are null and void, but the rule is applied to bills instrumental in assisting communication with an alien enemy rather than to every bill bearing an enemy's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have allowed liberal exceptions to enable, for example, English prisoners to use property at home for their support while detained (drawing subsistence bills). Bills void as instruments of trade with the enemy may nevertheless form the basis of a promise binding on return of peace. Attempts to structure bills to 'pass muster' (e.g., drawers, indorsements) are scrutinized to prevent enabling alien enemies to benefit from property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of war on contracts made before the war
rubrics_metrics.description: If performance of a contract previously entered into is rendered unlawful by the Government entering into war, the contract is dissolved on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: affreightment is dissolved when the voyage becomes unlawful; capture causing complete defeat dissolves contract despite recapture; blockade rendering delivery impossible dissolves contract. Temporary interruptions (embargoes, hostile blockades, investments of port of departure) are usually temporary impediments only. If an embargo is imposed by the merchant's own government as reprisal and the voyage's object is likely defeated (e.g., perishable cargo), merchant may end contract. In some cases the remedy is only suspended until termination of war (e.g., many executed contracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnerships dissolved by public war — prospective effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A Public War operates as a positive dissolution of Partnerships between subjects of the contending nations; the partnership is dissolved as to future operations but continues for antecedent engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By declaration of war respective subjects become enemies and cannot carry on lawful commercial intercourse or make valid contracts; property is mutually liable to capture. No notice is necessary to complete the dissolution (it occurs by operation of law). Peace does not fully restore extinguished co-partnerships except for matters existing prior to the war. Domicile of the partnership matters: a partnership domiciled in a neutral country with all partners resident there is treated as neutral, but if one or more partners domiciled in enemy country their shares are liable to capture even if the partnership establishment is neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading with the enemy punishable — historical criminal rule and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Trading with the Enemy was historically an indictable offence and at times a misdemeanor at common law (e.g., carrying corn to an enemy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiralty courts have applied strict interdiction, even to prohibit supplies to a British Colony partially subject to the enemy and in want of provisions. Cartel (truce) ships are subject to interdiction rules except limited exceptions (e.g., ransom bills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domicile as the test of nationality in war
rubrics_metrics.description: Domicile is generally the test of nationality; whether a person is treated as neutral or enemy depends on domicile (with exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The animus manendi (intention to remain or settle) is decisive. Temporary visits for health or transient business do not typically create domicile, though a special-purpose residence may mature into a general residence over time. Involuntary or constrained residence, however long, does not change original character. Acts evidencing domicile include removal, settlement, engagement in trade, payment of taxes. The intention must be disclosed or evidenced by acts. Native character may revert on intent to return. For intended removal it's advisable to apply to Government for a special pass rather than rely on intention alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile character may be acquired by trade (commercial domicile)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national character may be acquired by trade or commercial domicile: habitual trade in the enemy's country can stamp a hostile character on the individual's property independent of personal domicile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons habitually carrying on trade in enemy territory should be given time to withdraw; immediate confiscation would unduly burden neutrals. If a person enters or continues a house of trade in the enemy country during the war, residence in a neutral country will not protect his share in that house. Lawful trade unconnected to the belligerent country is exonerated, but where trade can be traced to the belligerent country it may be condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — colonial/coasting trade liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'rule of 1756' holds that neutrals engaged in branches of commerce confined in peace to subjects of the enemy (e.g., colonial or coasting trade) are liable to penal consequences of confiscation if they engage in those trades in war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine arose in the war of 1756 and penalizes neutral participation in trades that were closed to them in peacetime.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character of ships — owner residence and conduct determine flag
rubrics_metrics.description: When nothing special in a vessel's conduct applies, the national character of a ship is determined by the residence of the owner; but conduct (e.g., navigating under another state's pass) can change that character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ship navigating under the pass of a foreign country is considered as bearing that nation's character. A vessel purchased in the enemy's country and habitually employed in that country's trade from the commencement and during the war is deemed a ship of that country. Parties taking a pass and flag of another country cannot later rely against that flag; they face double disadvantage when assuming foreign flag and pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo treated separately from ship for national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Cargo and ship may bear distinct national characters; goods have no necessary dependence upon the authority (flag) of the ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some countries treat flag and pass as conclusive on cargo too, but in England goods can be differently considered. If cargo is laden in peace and documented as foreign property, sailing under foreign flag has not been held conclusive as to the cargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile property cannot be transferred in transitu
rubrics_metrics.description: Property which has a hostile character at the commencement of a voyage cannot change that character by assignment while it is in transitu so as to protect it from capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In peace transfers in transitu are possible, but in war courts hold that property continues as it was at shipment until actual delivery, preventing fraudulent transfers that would shield enemy goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects and conduct of war — necessity and humanity as limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawfulness of acts in war is limited by necessity; necessity is the measure of violence in war and humanity should temper its exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vattel: the end of a just war is to avenge or prevent injury; the lawfulness of the end only justifies bare means necessary for attainment. Acts beyond necessity are condemnable. Earlier writers claimed nearly unlimited licence; modern law (Grotius, Montesquieu) rejects practices like poisoned arms, assassins, violence to women or the dead, or murder of prisoners in cold blood. The rights of war are to be measured by the objects of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartels and exchanges of prisoners regulated by convention
rubrics_metrics.description: System of Cartels for exchange of prisoners arises from humanitarian views; exchanges are generally regulated by special convention between hostile states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prisoners may be permitted to return home on condition not to serve again until exchanged; officers may be released on parole with similar conditions. Commissaries may be permitted to reside in hostile states to carry out arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisoners of war — status and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A Prisoner of War is not adhering to the King's enemies and is under the King's protection; he may contract and is allowed to support himself and apply his trade, and may maintain actions for wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier cases held prisoners could not contract, but modern practice recognizes their need to subsist. A prisoner in confinement is protected as to person; if on parole he has protection in his credit and may sue for necessary support without being compelled to give security for costs as other foreigners might.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mariners' national character follows their service
rubrics_metrics.description: A mariner generally takes the character of the country in whose service he is employed; occasional visits to place of birth do not restore a neutral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if his wife and family reside in his native country, regular employment in the enemy's service and trade determines his national character; habitual employment outweighs mere visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of married foreigners — wife's allegiance and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A wife generally follows the country and allegiance of her husband, but exceptions exist where she is in the country of her birth or present by necessity; foreign ladies who marry Englishmen are naturalized and cease to be enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a wife is in the country by necessity or owing allegiance by birth and husband is an alien enemy unable to live here, the law gives her privileges of an unmarried woman so she may sue and be sued and contract for maintenance. Chief Justice Holt compared this to ladies allowed to sue upon adjurations or banishments of their lords.
